text.p: Here are the key facts on Zambia, where controversial presidential and parliamentary elections will be held on Monday:

POPULATION: 8.7 million (1992), from 73 ethnic groups. The biggest is the Bemba tribe in the north. Zambia is amongst the most urbanised countries in Africa with over 40 percent living in towns and cities. Its population is growing at 3.5 percent annally.
CAPITAL: Lusaka, population of about one million in 1990. Other major towns are Ndola and Kitwe on the Copperbelt.
AREA: 752,614 sq km. Landlocked, it borders (clockwise from north) Zaire, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia and Angola.
ARMED FORCES: Army - 15,000 men, 30 tanks; Airforce - 1,200 men, 25 fighter jets; Paramilitary Police - 1,200 men.

ECONOMY: Zambia is one of the world's poorest and most debt-ridden countries, but also one of the biggest producers of copper and cobalt, accounting for over 90 percent of foreign exchange revenue, though production has fallen steadily.

President Frederick Chiluba, who took over from socialist- oriented Kenneth Kaunda in 1991, sped up free-market reforms and has privatised about half the state-owned concerns, but the biggest -- copper producer ZCCM -- is still to come.
His reforms, after decades of command economy, government- set commodity prices and exchange controls, have won accolades from the World Bank but brought hardship for ordinary Zambians.
Inflation is still running at some 50 percent a year but the foreign debt of $6.4 billion is Zambia's biggest burden.
It will start to hurt more since foreign aid donors froze balance of payments support this year in protest at legal changes by the government seen as damaging democracy.
The average per capita income is $350.
Zambia has been a food deficit country since 1992, when most of southern Africa was hit by drought.
MODERN HISTORY: The former British protectorate of Northern Rhodesia became independent on October 24, 1964.
Kaunda, who headed the ruling United National Independence Party (UNIP) governed virtually unopposed for 27 years.
He introduced one-party rule in 1973. He stood for the presidency unopposed until the end of the Cold War and collapse of Soviet-led communism forced him to agree to free elections.
He lost in October 1991 to veteran trade unionist Chiluba, of the main opposition Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.
In 1995, Kaunda reentered politics after a three-year retirement when he was elected president of UNIP.
Unemployment and inflation were the opposition's main campaign weapons against the MMD, with Kaunda promising to reintroduce subsidies and stop privatisation.
But Kaunda's banning from the presidential race under disputed legal changes turned democracy itself into the core issue in a poll boycotted by UNIP and several other parties.
